annealed specimens mainly included ferrite
( \alpha ) ,

The dissolution temperature
for κ-carbide is between 850 °C and 900 °C. At the annealing temperature of
7 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,
all the γ phase transformed
to α phase and κ-carbide by eutectoid reaction. As the annealing temperature rose from 700 °C to 900
{ } ^ { \circ } C , \alpha
phase
and κ-carbide fraction decreased and γ phase fraction increased, and ultimate elongation increased, while ulti-

3. Results
3.1. Equilibrium phase diagram
The phase diagram of the Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C steel was calculated
by Thermo-Calc software with database TCFE7, and fractions of the
equilibrium phases (ferrite (α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide (κ)) when
the temperature is over
5 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
are shown in Fig. 2. According to Fig. 2,
ferrite is expected to form first during solidification, and then austenite
forms by peritectic reaction [33]. After solidification, the phase fraction
of ferrite will decrease and that of austenite will increase with the de-
crease of temperature until the temperature reaches around
1 0 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,
where the fraction of ferrite is lowest. When the temperature is lower
than about
1 0 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,
the fraction of ferrite decreases with the decrease
of temperature. However, the phase fractions do not change much
until temperature becomes lower than
8 2 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,
, where κ-carbide appears
by eutectoid reaction
\gamma  \alpha + \kappa .
Apparently, a part of body-centered
cubic (BCC) ferrite will always exist without transforming to face-
centered (FCC) austenite, and this part of ferrite is often referred to as
δ-ferrite [34,35]. The δ-ferrite usually exhibits coarse grains in the mi-
crostructure [13,34]. In the present study, δ-ferrite is not separately
treated with α-ferrite. There is difference in the phase fractions and
the eutectoid temperature for κ-carbide between the result calculated
by Thermo-Calc and that measured from the steel, which will discussed
later. The differences may come from that, the steel in the study is not in
equilibrium state, and that the calculated fractions are based on the
atomic fraction, while the measured fraction from XRD results is based
on the volume fraction [34].

5. Conclusions
In the present study, a Mn-lean Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel with
the chemical composition Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C (wt.%) is annealed at
the temperature range
7 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
to 1200 °C for 1 h. The microstructure
evolution during annealing and the relationship between tensile prop-
erties and microstructure of the annealed specimens are investigated.
(1) The density of the steel is 6.80 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, about 13% lower than that
of pure iron. The largest product of strength and ductility,
31 GPa%, is achieved at the annealing temperature of
9 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } ,
when the ultimate strength, yield strength, and ultimate elonga-
tion are 855 MPa, 651 MPa and 36.6%, respectively.
(2) The phases presented in the annealed steel mainly include ferrite
(α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide (κ). The dissolution temperature
of κ-carbide is between 850 °C and 900 °C. When annealed at 700
{ } ^ { \circ } { \mathsf { C } } ,
γ phase transforms to κ-carbide with lamellar morphology
and α phase by eutectoid reaction. With the increase of temper-
ature, the γ phase fraction first increases, and reaches largest,
about 63% at around
1 0 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
, and then decreases slightly. The
boundary κ-carbide formed during quenching exists in all the
specimens annealed at the range
9 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
to
1 2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .
Generally,
the α grains and γ grains grow up quickly when the annealing
temperature is over 900 °C.
(3) The ultimate strength of the annealed specimens has a decreas-
ing trend with the increase of temperature, while the ultimate
elongation first increases until anneal temperature reaches 900
{ } ^ { \circ } \mathbb { C } ,
and then decreases with the continued increase of tempera-
ture. The change of ultimate strength is sharp, so the window
for controlling the tensile properties is relatively small.
(4) At the annealing temperature between
7 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
and 900 °C, the
ductility of the specimens is mainly controlled by the fraction
of γ phase. Although the κ-carbide can contribute to the strength,
microcracks preferred to initiate around κ-carbide, which is det-
rimental to the tensile properties. At the annealing temperature
between
9 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }
and
1 2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } _ { \cdot }
, since the change of phase fractions
is very moderate, the grain sizes, instead of phase fraction
change, have a significant effect on the tensile properties. The ul-
timate strength and ultimate elongation both decrease with the
increase of grain sizes when increasing the annealing
temperature.

5. Conclusions
In the present study, a Mn-lean Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel with
the chemical composition Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C (wt.%) is annealed at
the temperature range
7 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
to 1200 °C for 1 h. The microstructure
evolution during annealing and the relationship between tensile prop-
erties and microstructure of the annealed specimens are investigated.
(1) The density of the steel is 6.80 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, about 13% lower than that
of pure iron. The largest product of strength and ductility,
31 GPa%, is achieved at the annealing temperature of
9 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } ,
when the ultimate strength, yield strength, and ultimate elonga-
tion are 855 MPa, 651 MPa and 36.6%, respectively.
(2) The phases presented in the annealed steel mainly include ferrite
(α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide (κ). The dissolution temperature
of κ-carbide is between 850 °C and 900 °C. When annealed at 700
{ } ^ { \circ } { \mathsf { C } } ,
γ phase transforms to κ-carbide with lamellar morphology
and α phase by eutectoid reaction. With the increase of temper-
ature, the γ phase fraction first increases, and reaches largest,
about 63% at around
1 0 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
, and then decreases slightly. The
boundary κ-carbide formed during quenching exists in all the
specimens annealed at the range
9 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
to
1 2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .
Generally,
the α grains and γ grains grow up quickly when the annealing
temperature is over 900 °C.
(3) The ultimate strength of the annealed specimens has a decreas-
ing trend with the increase of temperature, while the ultimate
elongation first increases until anneal temperature reaches 900
{ } ^ { \circ } \mathbb { C } ,
and then decreases with the continued increase of tempera-
ture. The change of ultimate strength is sharp, so the window
for controlling the tensile properties is relatively small.
(4) At the annealing temperature between
7 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
and 900 °C, the
ductility of the specimens is mainly controlled by the fraction
of γ phase. Although the κ-carbide can contribute to the strength,
microcracks preferred to initiate around κ-carbide, which is det-
rimental to the tensile properties. At the annealing temperature
between
9 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }
and
1 2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } _ { \cdot }
, since the change of phase fractions
is very moderate, the grain sizes, instead of phase fraction
change, have a significant effect on the tensile properties. The ul-
timate strength and ultimate elongation both decrease with the
increase of grain sizes when increasing the annealing
temperature.
